title: Coordination services: ZooKeeper, etcd and KRaft
goal: By the end, you can explain why programs hand their agreement to a small coordination service such as ZooKeeper or etcd, use its four tools to elect a leader, find the running copies of a program and take a lock, and stop a frozen leader with a fencing token.
opening:
Picture the ticket machine at a busy post office. You pull ticket 47. When it lights up, it's your turn, and nobody else's. Wander off, and the screen moves on to 48.

The payments app has a machine like that. Each night, one program pays every shop what it took that day. Three copies of it run on three machines, and a small service gives the turn to one of them. One night, copy A freezes for 15 seconds. The service decides A has wandered off, and B gets the turn and pays the shops. Then A wakes and pays them again.

It's easy to trust the turn. Inside one program, a lock means one holder at a time, and a service's lock sounds like the same promise. But a frozen program can't notice that its turn has ended.

Consensus with Raft built agreement among a few servers. In this lesson, we'll borrow it from a small service, etcd, and find the one check that stops the second payout. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Three copies of the nightly payout job pick a leader through etcd, a small service that hands out leadership. Leadership lasts 10 seconds unless the leader renews it. The leader, copy A, freezes for 15 seconds, so etcd ends its leadership, and copy B takes over and pays the shops. When A wakes, it writes its own payouts to the payout table. What can stop that write?
options: etcd: it ended A's leadership, so A's write fails
A's own connection to etcd: it knows the leadership ended and blocks the write
Only the payout table, if each write carries a number from the election that grows with every new leader, and the table refuses a number lower than one it has already seen
Raft: A's term is lower than B's
warmup.why: The write goes from A straight to the payout table. etcd isn't on that path and never sees it, which rules out the first option. A's own code can't help either: A checked it was leader before it froze, and a frozen program gets no signal that time passed. Only the receiver of the write can refuse it, and it needs a number that grows with every new leader to do so. Raft's terms belong to etcd's own servers, not to the programs that use etcd.

sections.h: Why programs borrow agreement: a small service and four tools
sections.body:
Look at what Consensus with Raft needed: a vote rule, a commit rule, a membership rule, and a bug that hid in the membership rule for about a year. Yet most programs need agreement on only a few facts. Which copy of the payout job pays tonight? Which copies of the fraud check, the program that looks for suspicious payments, are running, and where? Which machine holds which slice of the data? Building consensus into every program, to agree on a few thousand bytes, is the wrong trade.

Google drew that conclusion in its Chubby paper (2006). The team built a lock service rather than a Paxos library, because programmers found a lock and a small file far easier to use correctly than a consensus protocol. (A lock is a marker that only one holder may have at a time.) Chubby runs on five servers using Paxos, and its users hold locks for hours or days, not milliseconds. Free, open-source versions followed: ZooKeeper from Yahoo!, etcd from CoreOS and Consul from HashiCorp.

They're called **coordination services**, and the programs that use one are its clients. They share a shape. They're small: three or five servers, the data kept in memory, kilobytes to megabytes of it. Their data changes slowly: "job A pays tonight" changes every few minutes or hours, not thousands of times a second. And every write goes through consensus, so every change has one place in one order.

Think of the post office's ticket machine again. Its numbers only go up, the screen calls the lowest ticket still waiting, and if you leave, your number is skipped. A coordination service stores keys and values, and adds four tools that work the same way:

- compare-and-set: "create this key only if it doesn't exist yet", which exactly one caller wins (consensus in disguise, as Total order broadcast and the many faces of consensus showed);
- a counter that grows with every change, like the ticket numbers: the zxid in ZooKeeper, the revision in etcd;
- sessions: a client sends a heartbeat now and then to show it's alive, and keys tied to its session, called ephemeral keys, vanish when it stops, like a skipped ticket;
- watches: the service tells you when a key changes, so you don't keep asking.

Electing a leader, finding which copies of a program are running, and taking a lock are each a short recipe built from these four. The figure is the picture to keep. A small consensus group sits in the middle, with clients around it holding sessions. The thing they protect sits off to one side, and that's where the last check has to happen.

Where the picture breaks: a clerk can see you at the counter, but a coordination service sees only heartbeats, and a frozen program sends none, exactly like a dead one.

Agreement has the usual price. Every write is a consensus write, so adding servers makes writes slower. ZooKeeper's write rate, pushed to its limit, fell from 21,000 a second on 3 servers to 8,000 on 13, while reads, which each server answers from its own copy, rose. etcd's published test, three servers on rented cloud machines, puts one client's write at 1.6 ms and an up-to-date read at 0.7 ms.

Next, we'll open ZooKeeper, the oldest of the free ones, and meet the four tools in its own words.

sections.h: ZooKeeper: a tree of small nodes, sessions and one-shot watches
sections.body:
ZooKeeper stores a tree of small entries called **znodes**, named like file paths on a computer: `/election`, `/election/n-0000000003`, `/config/fees`. Each holds a few bytes or kilobytes. A group of three or five ZooKeeper servers, called an ensemble, copies every write with Zab, ZooKeeper's own leader-based protocol. Total order broadcast and the many faces of consensus put Zab in the same family as Raft.

Every change gets a zxid, a 64-bit number that grows with each write. (Its high half is the leader's epoch, like a Raft term, and its low half counts the writes within it.) Every znode records the zxid that created it (`cZxid`), a version number for its data, and a version number for its list of children (`cversion`).

Two options on `create` turn the tree into a coordination tool. An ephemeral znode belongs to the session that created it, and is deleted when that session ends. A sequential znode gets a counter from its parent added to its name, ten digits long. Create `/election/n-` three times and you get `n-0000000000`, `n-0000000001` and `n-0000000002`. The counter only goes up, even after the nodes are gone, like the ticket machine.

A session is how ZooKeeper notices that a client has died. The client connects to any server and sends heartbeats. The session timeout is agreed between 2 and 20 times the server's `tickTime`, which is 2 seconds by default, so between 4 and 40 seconds. The ensemble, not the client, decides when a session has expired, and then deletes its ephemeral znodes. A client that crashes without closing its session leaves its znodes in place until the timeout runs out, as the Try it shows.

A watch is a one-shot alert. Read a znode, or list its children, with the watch option set, and the server sends one event the next time that data or child list changes. Then the watch is gone. More can change between the event and your next read, and a disconnected client misses events. So every recipe reads the state again instead of trusting the event. ZooKeeper 3.6 added persistent, recursive watches that stay in place.

Reads come from whichever server the client is connected to, out of that server's own copy. So reads get faster as servers are added, but they can be stale, behind the latest write. Writes are linearizable: they behave as if there were one copy, in the sense of Linearizability: one copy, one timeline. A client that must see the latest write calls `sync` first.

The lock recipe from the ZooKeeper paper puts the pieces together. Create `/lock/n-` as ephemeral and sequential, then list the children. If yours is the lowest, you hold the lock. If not, watch only the node right before yours, and check again when it goes. When the holder dies, exactly one waiter wakes up. In the naive version, every waiter watches the holder, and 100 waiters wake up to find that 99 of them lost: the herd effect. Nobody writes this by hand in Java. Apache Curator, a Java library for ZooKeeper, ships it as `InterProcessMutex`, and leader election as `LeaderLatch` and `LeaderSelector`.

etcd offers the same four tools, with one change that fixes the missed events. Next, we'll see it.

try.title: Watch ephemeral nodes outlive a crashed client
steps: Start ZooKeeper (the official image is at 3.9.6). Then define a helper, `zk`, that runs one command of `zkCli.sh`, ZooKeeper's command-line client, and keeps only the interesting lines: `docker run -d --name sfz-zk -m 512m zookeeper:3.9.6`, wait five seconds, then `zk() { docker exec sfz-zk zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 "$@" 2>&1 | grep -E '^(Created|\[|cZxid|ephemeralOwner|cversion)'; }`.

Create the parent and two ephemeral sequential znodes, list them, and look at one. Their values, pod-a and pod-b, are only labels for two copies of a program (pod is a common name for one running copy). Each `zk` call is a client that exits without closing its session, like a program that crashed.
Predict what `ls /election` shows 40 seconds later, and what name the next sequential znode gets. Then run the last three commands.

Watches: open a second terminal window with `docker exec -it sfz-zk zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181` and type `ls -w /election`. In the first terminal, run `zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-d` twice. Count the events the second terminal prints. Stop with `docker rm -f sfz-zk`.

code.title: in any terminal
code.src:
zk create /election ""
zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-a
zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-b
zk ls /election
zk stat /election/n-0000000000
sleep 40
zk ls /election
zk stat /election
zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-c

try.expect:
```text
$ zk create /election ""
Created /election
$ zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-a
Created /election/n-0000000000
$ zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-b
Created /election/n-0000000001
$ zk ls /election
[n-0000000000, n-0000000001]
$ zk stat /election/n-0000000000
cZxid = 0x4
cversion = 0
ephemeralOwner = 0x1000038624e0001
(40 s later)
$ zk ls /election
[]
$ zk stat /election
cZxid = 0x2
cversion = 4
ephemeralOwner = 0x0
$ zk create -e -s /election/n- pod-c
Created /election/n-0000000002
```

The two znodes outlived the clients that made them. `ephemeralOwner` names a session, and the ensemble keeps a session until its timeout runs out with no heartbeat. `zkCli.sh` asks for 30 seconds, so after 40 both are gone. The parent's `cversion` of 4 counts two creates and two deletes, and the next sequential name is `n-0000000002`: the counter never reuses a number. The owner id and zxids differ on your machine. In the watching terminal, you see one event, `WatchedEvent state:SyncConnected type:NodeChildrenChanged path:/election`, for the first create, and nothing for the second: the watch fired once and was gone.

sections.h: etcd: one change counter, leases and watches you can resume
sections.body:
etcd spells the same four tools differently. Its current release is 3.7.3. Keys are flat strings, and a shared beginning such as `/svc/payments/` plays the part of a folder. Three or five members, as etcd calls its servers, copy every write with Raft, through the same etcd-io/raft library that Consensus with Raft mentioned.

The counter is the **revision**, one number for the whole cluster. It goes up by one for every change, or for every transaction (a group of changes made as one step), however many keys that touches. Each key remembers its `create_revision`, its `mod_revision` (its last change) and its `version` (how many times it has changed since it was created). etcd keeps old versions of each key until a clean-up called compaction removes them. So you can read a key as it was at revision 2, and you can start a watch from a past revision. That makes watches resumable. A client that was disconnected asks for every change after revision 1,042 and misses nothing, unless compaction has already thrown those revisions away. ZooKeeper's one-shot watches can't do that.

Compare-and-set is a transaction: a list of comparisons, the operations to run if they all hold, and the operations to run if not. "If the `create_revision` of `/leader` is 0, which means the key doesn't exist, put `/leader pod-a`" is one caller winning, in one line. Two programs that send it at the same moment get one SUCCESS and one FAILURE.

Sessions are leases: grants that last a set time unless they're renewed. A client asks for a lease with a time to live (TTL), attaches keys to it, and keeps it alive with heartbeats, which etcd calls keep-alives. When the TTL passes without one, etcd ends the lease and deletes every key attached to it, and each deletion is a change with its own revision. Watches report PUT and DELETE events for a key or a shared beginning, in revision order and never twice. They aren't linearizable, though: etcd's documentation says delivery takes about 10 ms in a healthy cluster, with no upper limit in an unhealthy one.

Reads are up to date by default, served through ReadIndex from Consensus with Raft: the leader checks with a majority before it answers. What etcd calls a serializable read is answered by any member from its own copy. (The name is confusing: here it means only that the read sees the data as of one revision, which may be an old one.) It's faster, 0.3 ms against 0.7 ms for one client in etcd's test, and it may be stale.

etcd's client library for Go, a programming language, wraps all of this in a `Session` (a lease kept alive, 60 seconds by default), a `Mutex` (a lock) and an `Election`. The `etcdctl lock` and `etcdctl elect` commands are built on them. jetcd, the official Java client, offers the same lock and election tools.

With these tools, the everyday jobs become short recipes. Next, we'll elect a leader with them, and freeze it.

try.title: Revisions, compare-and-set and a lease running out
steps: Start a one-member etcd 3.7.3, and a short name for its command-line tool, etcdctl: `docker run -d --name sfz-etcd -m 512m gcr.io/etcd-development/etcd:v3.7.3 etcd --listen-client-urls http://0.0.0.0:2379 --advertise-client-urls http://localhost:2379`, then `alias ectl='docker exec -i sfz-etcd etcdctl'`.
Write a key twice, read it with all its fields, then read it as it was at revision 2.
Run the same compare-and-set for two candidates, named pod-a and pod-b. Predict which one wins.

In a second terminal, start `docker exec sfz-etcd etcdctl watch --prefix /svc/payments`. Grant a 10-second lease, register pod-a's address under it, and wait 10 seconds without renewing it. Keep `sfz-etcd` running for the next Try it.

code.title: in any terminal
code.src:
ectl put /config/fx-rate 1.09
ectl put /config/fx-rate 1.10
ectl get /config/fx-rate -w fields
ectl get /config/fx-rate --rev=2
printf 'create("/leader") = "0"

put /leader pod-a


' | ectl txn
printf 'create("/leader") = "0"

put /leader pod-b

get /leader

' | ectl txn
ectl lease grant 10
ectl put --lease=<lease id from the line above> /svc/payments/pod-a 10.0.0.5:8080

try.expect:
```text
$ ectl get /config/fx-rate -w fields
"ClusterID" : 14841639068965178418
"MemberID" : 10276657743932975437
"Revision" : 3
"RaftTerm" : 2
"Key" : "/config/fx-rate"
"CreateRevision" : 2
"ModRevision" : 3
"Version" : 2
"Value" : "1.10"
"Lease" : 0
"More" : false
"Count" : 1
$ ectl get /config/fx-rate --rev=2
/config/fx-rate
1.09
$ ... | ectl txn        (pod-a)
SUCCESS

OK
$ ... | ectl txn        (pod-b)
FAILURE

/leader
pod-a
$ ectl lease grant 10
lease 694da1b9e3d39309 granted with TTL(10s)
$ ectl put --lease=694da1b9e3d39309 /svc/payments/pod-a 10.0.0.5:8080
OK
```

and in the watching terminal, the second event about 10 seconds after the first:

```text
PUT
/svc/payments/pod-a
10.0.0.5:8080
DELETE
/svc/payments/pod-a
```

The cluster started at revision 1, and each put raised it by one: the key was created at 2 and last changed at 3, its second version. Revision 2 is still stored, so the old value comes back. pod-a's transaction found no `/leader` and wrote it. pod-b's comparison failed, so its other branch read who had won. Nobody renewed the lease, so etcd deleted the key when the 10 seconds ran out, and the watch reported it. That's how finding running copies notices a dead one. The cluster and member ids and the lease id differ on your machine; the revisions don't.

sections.h: Electing a leader, and fencing the one that froze
sections.body:
Here's the payout job again. Three copies, A, B and C, run on three machines, and only one may pay the shops each night. Payments people call that nightly payout settlement, which is why the election in the Try it is named `settlement`. The payout ledger is the table where each payout is recorded.

Leader election: every candidate creates a key under one shared name, attached to its own lease. The key with the lowest `create_revision` (in ZooKeeper, the lowest sequence number) is the leader, the post office's lowest ticket. Every other candidate watches the key right before its own. That's what etcd's `Election` and Curator's `LeaderLatch` do.

Finding running copies, which is called service discovery, works the same way. Each copy registers a key such as `/svc/payments/pod-a`, holding its network address, under a lease. Programs that want to call it list the keys and watch them. This doesn't need up-to-date reads. A list one second old is fine, because callers must cope with a copy that died a moment ago anyway. So reads from a member's own copy, plus a local list kept current by a watch, are the right choice.

Work assignment is the same. Members register under leases, and the leader writes one key saying who handles which slice of the work. It uses a compare-and-set on that key's `mod_revision`, so two leaders can't overwrite each other's plan.

A lock is leader election for one resource, and here the danger from Leases, locks and fencing tokens, in the Faults, time and truth track, comes back. A lease only says who should hold the lock. It can't stop a holder that froze past its lease from acting when it wakes. Java programs freeze like that during garbage collection (GC), when the JVM, the program that runs Java code, pauses everything to clean up memory.

In 2020, Jepsen, a project that tests databases by breaking them on purpose, tested etcd 3.4.3. Its reads and writes behaved correctly in every test, and its locks didn't. With leases of 1 to 3 seconds, two holders overlapped within minutes, even in a healthy cluster. With 2-second leases, about 18% of confirmed updates to a lock-protected set were lost. Jepsen's answer is **fencing**: every write carries a number, and the resource refuses old ones.

Here the token comes free. The leader key's `create_revision` was handed out by consensus, so no two leaders share one, and every new leader's is higher. The resource stores the highest token it has accepted and refuses any lower one, like a clerk who has called 48 and won't serve ticket 47. Chubby called this a sequencer; in ZooKeeper, the znode's `cZxid` does the job. The stepper plays it out with a 15-second freeze, and the lab builds it.

One rule keeps it honest. The check must happen at the resource, in the same all-or-nothing step as the write. A payout table that checks the token in one step and writes in the next has reopened the gap. In a SQL database that means one conditional statement, which the worked example shows.

**A lease says who should act. Only the resource can refuse the one who shouldn't.** Next, we'll see the same tools built into Kafka, and how coordination services themselves fail.

Each created a key tied to its own 10-second lease: A's key got revision 7, B's 9 and C's 11 (other writes took the numbers between). **The lowest revision leads**, so job A leads, and 7 is its fencing token. B watches A's key and C watches B's: one watcher per key, so no herd.

frames.say: A wakes and finishes what it was doing when it froze: it writes a payout with token 7. It checked that it was leader before the freeze, and nothing has told it otherwise. **The ledger refuses: 7 is lower than 9.** Without that check, two copies would have written payouts, and the shops in batch 17 could be paid twice.

frames.say: A's next keep-alive fails: the lease is gone. Now it knows it lost, so it **rejoins at the back** with a new lease and a new key, revision 13, and watches C's key. A token never comes back down: if C leads next, its token is 11, and A's would be 13.

stepper.intro: Three copies of the payout job, A, B and C, elect a leader through etcd. Use Next and Back, or the arrow keys.

try.title: Elect a leader with etcdctl, then crash it
steps: Keep `sfz-etcd` from the last Try it running. Each candidate runs as its own container that shares etcd's network, so `docker stop` is a clean shutdown and `docker kill` is a crash. The candidates' names, pod-a to pod-c, are only labels: `cand() { docker run -d --name sfz-$1 --network container:sfz-etcd --entrypoint etcdctl gcr.io/etcd-development/etcd:v3.7.3 elect settlement $1; }`.
Start pod-a, then pod-b. Read each one's log (`elect` prints the leader key once it leads), and list the keys with their create revisions.

Stop pod-a cleanly and read pod-b's log again. Then start pod-c, crash pod-b with `docker kill`, and time how long pod-c waits. Predict the wait first: `etcdctl elect` uses the Go client's default lease.
Clean up: `docker rm -f sfz-pod-a sfz-pod-b sfz-pod-c sfz-etcd`.

code.title: in any terminal
code.src:
cand pod-a; sleep 1; cand pod-b; sleep 2
docker logs sfz-pod-a; docker logs sfz-pod-b
ectl get --prefix settlement -w fields | grep -E '"Key"|"CreateRevision"|"Value"'
docker stop sfz-pod-a; sleep 1; docker logs sfz-pod-b
cand pod-c; sleep 2
date +%T; docker kill sfz-pod-b
until docker logs sfz-pod-c | grep -q pod-c; do sleep 1; done; date +%T

try.expect:
```text
$ docker logs sfz-pod-a
settlement/694da1b9e3d3930e
pod-a
$ docker logs sfz-pod-b
$ ectl get --prefix settlement -w fields | grep ...
"Key" : "settlement/694da1b9e3d3930e"
"CreateRevision" : 7
"Value" : "pod-a"
"Key" : "settlement/694da1b9e3d39313"
"CreateRevision" : 8
"Value" : "pod-b"
$ docker stop sfz-pod-a; sleep 1; docker logs sfz-pod-b
settlement/694da1b9e3d39313
pod-b
$ cand pod-c; sleep 2
$ date +%T; docker kill sfz-pod-b
23:41:50
$ until ...; date +%T
23:42:46
```

pod-a's key was created at revision 7 and pod-b's at 8, so pod-a led, and pod-b printed nothing: it was waiting on pod-a's key. Each key is named after its lease. A clean stop ends the lease, so pod-b took over within a second, with 8 as its fencing token. A crash ends nothing: pod-c waited 56 seconds, the rest of pod-b's 60-second lease, before it led with revision 10. That wait is the price of noticing failure by lease. A shorter lease buys a faster takeover, and more false alarms. The revisions follow from the last Try it's six changes; the lease names and times differ on your machine.

refs.title: Kleppmann: How to do distributed locking

aside.title: Couldn't the job check that it still leads, right before it writes?
aside.body: It can, and it should, but that only narrows the gap. The freeze can land between the check and the write, and from inside a frozen program the freeze is invisible: the next line of code runs as if no time had passed. Checking the clock has the same flaw, because the clock can be read before the freeze too. Only the receiver sees the write at the moment it arrives, so only the receiver can refuse it.

sections.h: Kafka's built-in coordinator, and how coordination services fail
sections.body:
Until version 3.9, Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages for other programs, used ZooKeeper for all of this. Each broker, as Kafka calls its servers, registered an ephemeral znode. The controller, the broker in charge of the cluster's records, was whichever broker created the ephemeral `/controller` znode first. That meant two distributed systems to run and upgrade, and a new controller had to read the cluster's records back out of ZooKeeper before it could act.

Kafka 4.0 (March 2025) removed ZooKeeper; the current release is 4.4.0. The controllers now run their own Raft group, the pull-based KRaft from Consensus with Raft, over the `__cluster_metadata` log. It's the same four tools, built in. Brokers register with the active controller and send it heartbeats, and the controller shuts out a broker that goes quiet: a session. Every change to the records is written at the next position, or offset, of the log: a revision. Brokers read the log and apply each change: a watch you can resume from any offset. Epochs fence old leaders: a message that carries an older epoch is refused, as the payout ledger refused token 7. The messages themselves are copied between brokers by a cheaper method, which the Messaging and logs track covers.

Coordination services fail too, and their failures spread, because everything leans on them. On 2 November 2020, a network switch at Cloudflare, a company that carries a large share of the web's traffic, failed partly for six minutes. It kept its links up but dropped some traffic. In a three-node etcd cluster, node 1 could no longer reach node 3, the leader, though node 2 reached both. Node 1 kept starting elections and node 2 kept voting for node 3, so the votes tied, and no leader that node 1 could reach was elected. While elections block, Raft accepts no writes, so etcd could only be read.

A tool that managed Cloudflare's databases checked the main database through etcd. It couldn't confirm the database was healthy, so it moved writes to an up-to-date copy, losing no data. But a bug made every other copy rebuild itself after the move. The database that checks logins was left with no copies to share its reads, and it was overloaded. For 6 hours and 33 minutes, as few as 75% of requests to Cloudflare's API (the interface its customers' programs call) succeeded. Its dashboard ran up to 80 times slower. Cloudflare first called it a Byzantine failure, one where a part lies; a postscript corrects that to an omission fault, where a part silently drops messages. Raft's PreVote and CheckQuorum, from the Go deeper notes of Consensus with Raft, aim at this kind of partial cut.

The client library is part of the system too. In 2024, Jepsen found that jetcd 0.6.0 to 0.8.2 retried transactions it had already sent when an answer was lost. A transaction that had committed ran a second time. Updates were lost, and a conditional transaction failed its own comparison on the rerun and was reported as failed, although it had committed. jetcd 0.8.5 retries only operations that are safe to repeat, by default. On older versions, set `retryMaxAttempts(0)` and handle retries yourself, with idempotency keys, labels that let the receiver spot a repeated request.

The lab builds a small coordination service and a fenced election, so you can freeze a leader yourself.

try.title: Read Raft's words off Kafka's controllers
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the three-node Kafka 4.4.0 cluster of the Messaging and logs track (about 2.3 GB; each node is both a broker and a voting controller): `docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml up -d --wait`.
Describe the controllers' status and replication. Match each field to a word from Consensus with Raft: term, commit index, leader, followers.
Stop the node that leads (yours may not be kafka-3: change the service name, and run the next commands on a node that is still up). Predict LeaderEpoch first, then describe the controllers again.
Optional: stop a second node and try `kafka-topics.sh --create`. Then `docker compose -f env/kafka-cluster.yml down -v`.

try.expect:
```text
ClusterId:              rCAfKEuEQVibTDqU5ooeSA
LeaderId:               3
LeaderEpoch:            1
HighWatermark:          67
MaxFollowerLag:         0
MaxFollowerLagTimeMs:   45
CurrentVoters:          [{"id": 1, ...}, {"id": 2, ...}, {"id": 3, ...}]   (trimmed)
CurrentObservers:       []

NodeId  ...  LogEndOffset  Lag  ...  Status
3       ...  69            0    ...  Leader
1       ...  69            0    ...  Follower
2       ...  69            0    ...  Follower
```

after stopping kafka-3:

```text

1       ...  97            0    ...  Leader
2       ...  97            0    ...  Follower
3       ...  -1            98   ...  Follower
```

LeaderEpoch is the term, and HighWatermark is the commit index: offset 67 of `__cluster_metadata` is on a majority. The three voters are the Raft group. CurrentObservers is empty because every node here is also a voter; brokers on their own would show up there. A clean stop hands leadership over at once, so `describe --status` now shows LeaderId 1 and LeaderEpoch 2, and the stopped node's offset reads -1. With a second node stopped, one voter is left, which is no majority, and a topic create waits about a minute and fails with a disconnect error. Offsets and the first leader differ from run to run. Output trimmed: directory ids and timestamps cut.

compare.title: The same four tools in ZooKeeper 3.9 and etcd 3.7

a.label: ZooKeeper
a.title: a tree of znodes, replicated with Zab
a.src:
compare-and-set  create(path) fails if it exists;
                 setData(path, data, version)
counter          zxid on every change; cZxid, version,
                 cversion per znode
session          client session, timeout 2 to 20 x tickTime;
                 EPHEMERAL znodes die with it
ordering         SEQUENTIAL znodes: n-0000000007
watch            one-shot per read; persistent and
                 recursive since 3.6
reads            local to the server (may be stale);
                 sync() first for the latest

b.label: etcd
b.title: flat keys with history, replicated with Raft
b.src:
compare-and-set  Txn: if create_revision(k) == 0 then put
                 else get
counter          one cluster revision per change;
                 create_revision, mod_revision, version
session          lease with a TTL, kept alive by the client;
                 attached keys die with it
ordering         create_revision of each key
watch            per key or prefix, from any revision
                 still kept (resumable)
reads            linearizable by default (ReadIndex);
                 serializable on request

compare.note: Both give you the same four tools, so the recipes look the same. The differences are in the details that bite. ZooKeeper's watches fire once and miss changes while you're disconnected, while etcd's resume from a revision until compaction removes it. ZooKeeper's reads come from the local copy unless you call sync, while etcd's are up to date unless you ask otherwise. In both, the number that orders changes (zxid or revision) is what makes a fencing token.

worked.title: Fence the payout table with the election revision

steps.say: The payout job's leader learns its token when it wins: the `create_revision` of its election key. With the Go client, that's `Election.Rev()`; with etcdctl, read the key's fields.
Give the payout database one row that remembers the highest token it has accepted, so the check lives at the resource.
steps.code:
CREATE TABLE payout_fence (id int PRIMARY KEY, token bigint NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO payout_fence VALUES (1, 0);

steps.say: Every payout transaction starts by moving the fence forward, in one conditional statement. A lower token updates no row.
The leader checks how many rows changed before it writes. Zero rows means a newer leader has written: roll back, which undoes the transaction, and stop acting as leader.

Replay the stepper with the Try it's numbers. pod-b (token 8) has written, so the fence holds 8. pod-a wakes with token 7: its UPDATE matches no row, it rolls back, and its payouts never reach the table. The lock the database takes on the fence row also puts two leaders that write at the same moment in order.
steps.code:
fence = 8
pod A:  UPDATE ... WHERE token <= 7   -> 0 rows -> rollback
pod B:  UPDATE ... WHERE token <= 8   -> 1 row  -> payouts written

lab.title: Build a coordination service and a fenced leader election
steps: Read `Coordinator.kt`: sessions, keep-alives, watches and `delete` are written for you. Everything runs on `Sim`'s pretend clock, so a minute of leases and pauses takes a few milliseconds, and every run comes out the same. Run the tests once: all 12 fail.

Write `Coordinator.create`: sequential names with `nextSequence`, the owning session (refuse an expired one), one new revision per create, and a CREATED event through `fire`. Then write `expire`. The five `CoordinatorTest` tests pass.
Write `Ledger.append` in `Election.kt`: refuse a token lower than the highest one accepted, and accept an equal or higher one. The first `ElectionTest` passes.

Write `Candidate.campaign` and `Candidate.check`, the ZooKeeper recipe: an ephemeral sequential node; lead if it's first, otherwise watch the node right before yours. The election tests pass, including the frozen leader whose late write the ledger refuses.

Run everything. `FencingPropertyTest` runs a few hundred random minutes of pauses (up to 8 seconds, against a 3-second lease) and crashes. The fenced ledger's tokens never go down, while most of the same runs without the fence let an old leader write after a newer one.
hints: The parent of `/election/n-` is `/election`: use `parentOf(path)`, and call `nextSequence` only for sequential creates, so `/locks/n-` keeps its own counter.
In `expire`, collect the paths first and delete afterwards: `delete` changes the map you would be looping over.
In `check`, look your own node up again with `coord.get`. After a long pause it may be gone, and then you aren't the leader, whatever `isLeader` said before.
Watch with `coord.watch(path) { onWatch() }`, not with `check()` directly: `onWatch` holds the check back while the process is paused, as a frozen JVM would.

drill.title: Write the election check from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write `check()` for a candidate that holds `node`, an ephemeral sequential node under `electionPath`. Step out if the node is gone. Lead, with the node's `createRevision` as the token, if it's first. Otherwise, watch only the node right before it.

recap: A coordination service is a small consensus group (3 or 5 servers, kilobytes in memory, facts that change slowly) that programs use instead of building consensus in. Google's Chubby (2006) set the pattern; ZooKeeper and etcd are the free versions most systems use.
Four tools do the work: compare-and-set, a counter on every change (zxid, revision), sessions whose ephemeral keys vanish when the client stops, and watches.

ZooKeeper: a tree of znodes, ephemeral and sequential options, sessions timed out by the ensemble, one-shot watches, and reads from the local copy unless you `sync`. etcd: flat keys with history, one revision for the cluster, leases, watches you can resume, and up-to-date reads by default.
Leader election and locks are the lowest-number-wins recipe, with one watcher per key. Service discovery is keys under a lease plus a watch, and slightly old reads are fine for it.

The limit: no lock gives one holder at a time on its own, because a frozen holder acts after its lease ends. Fence with the leader key's revision, checked by the resource in the same step as the write.
Kafka 4 runs the same four tools inside its KRaft controllers. In practice, coordination fails through partial network cuts (Cloudflare, 2020) and unsafe client retries (jetcd before 0.8.5).
closing:
We started at a post office's ticket machine, and a payout job that paid the shops twice. The service never got the turn wrong: etcd ended A's turn on time, and the frozen copy acted on a turn it no longer had. What stopped it was the check at the counter: the payout table refusing a token lower than one it had seen.

If you have Docker, run the election Try it again, but freeze pod-a with `docker pause sfz-pod-a` instead of stopping it, and time how long pod-b takes to lead.

Next, we'll build a whole SQL database out of many Raft groups, and ask how it puts transactions from many machines in one order when no two clocks agree.

quiz.q: A ZooKeeper lock has 200 waiting clients, and each one watches the lock holder's znode. The holder crashes. What happens, and what's the fix?
options: One waiter is woken at random, which is fair enough
All 200 wake up, all list the children, and 199 find they lost: watch only the znode right before your own
None wake up, because watches don't fire for ephemeral znodes
ZooKeeper queues the waiters itself and hands the lock to the next one
quiz.why: A watch fires for every client that set it, so 200 events go out, and 200 clients ask the ensemble at once to find that one of them won: the herd effect. With sequential znodes, each waiter only needs to know when the one right before it goes, so a crash wakes exactly one client. ZooKeeper itself hands out no locks, which rules out the last option: the recipe lives in the client, and that's why Curator exists.

quiz.q: A copy of the fraud check registers itself under `/svc/fraud/` with a 10-second etcd lease, and renews it every 3 seconds. Its machine loses power. When do other programs stop seeing it?
options: At once: etcd notices the network connection drop and deletes the key
When the program runs its shutdown code
About 10 seconds after its last renewal, when the lease runs out and etcd deletes the key, plus the time the watch takes to report it
Never: someone must delete the key by hand
quiz.why: A lease is a timer the client must keep resetting. A dead machine can't reset it, and can't run shutdown code either. etcd deletes the attached keys when the time runs out, as one change with its own revision, and watchers hear about it a little later (about 10 ms when the cluster is healthy, with no upper limit otherwise). The first option is tempting, but etcd goes by the lease, not the connection. The length is a trade: a shorter lease notices faster, and raises more false alarms when a program merely freezes.

quiz.q: Two copies of the payout job both believe they lead. A's election key has create_revision 120, and B's has 133. Both write to the payout table, which keeps a fence row. What must the table do to stay correct?
options: Accept both, since both copies hold a valid lease
Always refuse 133, because 120 was elected first
Refuse both until etcd confirms which one leads
Once it has accepted 133, refuse 120; before that, 120 may be accepted
quiz.why: The fence row remembers the highest token accepted and refuses lower ones. A's writes are fine until the newer leader has written. After that, A is a leftover leader that doesn't know it lost, and its token proves it. Asking etcd before every write, the third option, doesn't close the gap, because a freeze can still fall between etcd's answer and the write.

quiz.q: From Consensus with Raft: etcd answers a normal, up-to-date read only after its leader confirms with a majority that it still leads. A program that keeps track of another program's running copies lists their 300 addresses every second. What should it use, and why?
options: Reads from any member's own copy, or a watch plus a local list: a list a moment old is fine, because callers must handle a dead copy anyway, and it spares the leader a ReadIndex round per read
Up-to-date reads: a list of addresses must never be old
Writes, because only writes go through Raft
A lock around every read
quiz.why: ReadIndex costs a heartbeat round with a majority before every up-to-date read. Service discovery doesn't need that: a copy that died a second ago will fail its next request anyway, whatever the list said. A watch from a known revision keeps the local list current without asking again and again. Keep up-to-date reads for decisions where old data breaks a rule, such as who leads. The second option sounds safest, but it pays for a promise this job never uses.

quiz.q: A program uses jetcd 0.8.2 and runs a transaction: if the key `/batch/17/state` has mod_revision 50, set it to `paid`. The network loses the response, jetcd retries, and the call reports failure. What may really have happened?
options: Nothing was written: a failure means the transaction didn't commit
The first attempt committed; the retry found mod_revision no longer 50 and failed, so a committed transaction was reported as failed
etcd ran the transaction twice and stored `paid` twice
The lease expired
quiz.why: This is the anomaly Jepsen found in jetcd 0.6.0 to 0.8.2: a retry of a transaction that had already been applied. The first attempt raised the key's mod_revision, so the rerun's comparison failed, and the program saw failure. That's why the first option is wrong: a failure after a lost answer means 'unknown', not 'didn't happen'. Newer jetcd retries only operations that are safe to repeat. Otherwise, read the state again, or use an idempotency key, before deciding.

flashcards.front: What are the four tools of a coordination service?
flashcards.back: Compare-and-set, a counter on every change (zxid or revision), sessions with ephemeral keys, and watches.
A znode owned by a session. The ensemble deletes it when the session closes, or expires because no heartbeat arrived within the timeout.

flashcards.front: What does an etcd revision count?
flashcards.back: Changes to the whole cluster: every put, delete or transaction adds one. Each key keeps its create_revision, mod_revision and version.

flashcards.front: Why can an etcd watch resume, when a ZooKeeper watch can't?
flashcards.back: etcd keeps old revisions until compaction, so a client asks for every change after revision N. A ZooKeeper watch fires once, and events during a disconnect are lost.

flashcards.front: What makes a good fencing token from etcd or ZooKeeper?
flashcards.back: The leader key's create_revision (etcd) or the znode's cZxid (ZooKeeper). Consensus assigned it, so it's unique and higher for every new leader.

flashcards.front: What happened to Cloudflare's etcd in November 2020?
flashcards.back: A switch that failed partly cut node 1 off from the leader, node 3, but not from node 2. Elections tied, etcd took no writes, and the tools built on it turned six minutes into a six-hour outage.

terms.plain: A small store, copied by consensus (ZooKeeper, etcd, Consul), for a few slow-changing facts that many programs must agree on.
An entry in ZooKeeper's tree: a path with a little data, version numbers, and the zxid that created it.
A znode or key tied to a client's session or lease. It disappears when the client stops renewing.
A znode whose name gets its parent's next counter value added, such as n-0000000007.
etcd's change counter for the whole cluster. Every change gets the next one, and keys remember theirs.
A grant that lasts a set time unless the client renews it with heartbeats. etcd deletes the keys attached to it when it runs out.
A request to be told when a key, or a group of keys, changes.
A number that grows with every new leader or lock holder. The resource refuses any write that carries a lower number than one it has seen.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a friend why a leader elected through etcd can still write a wrong payout, and what exactly prevents it.
explain_back.answer: etcd elects a leader by giving each candidate a key under a lease. The lowest create revision leads, and if the leader stops renewing its lease, etcd deletes its key and the next candidate takes over. But the leader can freeze, for a long garbage collection, a stalled machine or a slow disk, between checking that it leads and writing. While it's frozen, its lease runs out, and another copy becomes leader and writes. When the first one wakes, nothing has told it, so it writes too, and two leaders have paid the same batch. etcd can't stop this, because the write doesn't go through etcd. The fix is a fencing token: the leader key's create revision, which consensus assigned and which is higher for every new leader. Each write carries it. The payout table keeps the highest token it has accepted, and refuses lower ones in the same statement as the write. The old leader's token is lower, so its write is refused.

deeper.body:
**Consul and Kubernetes leases.** Consul, HashiCorp's coordination service (Raft too), offers three read modes: `default`, which an old leader can still answer during an election; `consistent`, which checks leadership with a majority first; and `stale`, which any server answers, and which works without a majority. `stale` is the default for its DNS interface, the lookup system that turns names into addresses. Kubernetes, a system that runs programs across many machines, keeps all its state in etcd, and builds leader election on `Lease` objects stored there. Neither changes the fencing rule.

**Who else leans on ZooKeeper.** HBase, a database for very large tables, and Flink, a stream-processing system, in its high-availability mode, run on ZooKeeper; Kafka did until 3.9.

**Watches aren't a log.** A ZooKeeper watch fires once and says only that something changed. etcd's watch is ordered and resumable but not linearizable, and compaction limits how far back you can resume. For a reliable stream of changes, use a log (Kafka, or a database's change data capture, which the Stream processing track covers), and keep the coordination service for coordination.

**etcd 3.7.** The 3.7 release removed the old version 2 interface for good, along with the flags that had been marked experimental.

**How much to trust the lease.** Chubby added a lock-delay for clients that can't check sequencers: after a holder dies, the lock stays unavailable for up to a minute, so that its requests still in flight drain away. etcd's 3.7 release puts lease revocation first under overload, so that leases end on time. Both shrink the window; only a fencing check at the resource closes it. Chapter 10 of Designing Data-Intensive Applications describes these services as a way to hand consensus to a few servers, and lists their uses and limits.
